issues.legal_issue: A statutory power to exempt individual buildings from rent-control protections is constitutional when the legislation supplies sufficient guidance for exercising that power.
material_facts: The legislation regulated letting, controlled rents, and sought to prevent unreasonable eviction of tenants.
Its tenant protections could cause hardship to landlords or be abused by tenants, and the legislation provided a discretionary exemption power to address such circumstances.
issues.conclusion: The exemption power was not arbitrary or unguided and did not violate the constitutional guarantee of equal protection.
issues.legal_principle: Under Article 14, legislation may leave selection or classification to the government if the statute supplies a policy or principle guiding that discretion; executive action that fails to follow the guidance may be invalid even though the statute is valid. The preamble and operative provisions supplied adequate guidance here. The Court relied on Ram Krishna Dalmia v. Justice Tendolkar, [1959] SCR 279, and Sardar Inder Singh v. State of Rajasthan, [1957] SCR 605, which also referred to Harishanker Bagla v. State of Madhya Pradesh.

predicates.rent_control_case: The proceeding concerns legislation regulating rents and protecting tenants from unreasonable eviction.
predicates.statute_policy_is_stated: The legislation states its purposes and contains operative provisions that guide the exercise of the exemption discretion.
predicates.exemption_power_addresses_unforeseen_har: The legislation permits exemptions to address hardship or abuse that its general protections may produce.

issues.definition: When a rent-control proceeding involves a stated legislative policy and an exemption power directed to unforeseen hardship or abuse, the exemption power is constitutional.

issues.legal_issue: A party may challenge an adverse ruling on an issue when that ruling and the favorable judgment are parts of the same proceeding and the issue was not finally disposed of separately.
material_facts: The court had first addressed the constitutional challenge while leaving the pending appeal for further consideration on its merits.
The later decision in that same appeal granted relief on the merits, and the party seeking to preserve that relief challenged the earlier adverse conclusion without having separately appealed it.
issues.conclusion: The party was not precluded from challenging the constitutional ruling and could support the favorable judgment by contesting the adverse conclusion.
issues.legal_principle: Where successive rulings are parts of one continuing proceeding and the relevant matter was not finally disposed of separately, the party may challenge the adverse ruling when defending the favorable judgment; the Court also considered that it was doubtful a separate appeal would have lain from the earlier ruling.

predicates.same_proceeding: The earlier ruling and the later favorable judgment were made in the same continuing proceeding.
predicates.earlier_issue_not_finally_disposed: The court left the proceeding pending after its earlier ruling and later considered the matter further.
predicates.party_defends_favorable_judgment: A party seeks to preserve a favorable judgment by contesting an adverse ruling made during that proceeding.

issues.definition: If a party defends a favorable judgment in the same proceeding in which the earlier issue remained open, the party may challenge the adverse ruling.

issues.legal_issue: An individual exemption from tenant protections is invalid when the reasons supporting it are not relevant to the legislation’s purpose and relevant circumstances have not been considered.
material_facts: A tenant had accepted a fixed-term lease after declining an offered longer lease and remained in possession after the term expired, relying on statutory protection.
The government exempted the building based on the tenant’s choice of a shorter lease, the expiry of the lease, the tenant’s other businesses, and the tenant’s continued possession.
The government did not consider whether the tenant could obtain alternative premises to continue the business conducted in the building.

The majority held that the tenant’s continued possession and exercise of statutory rights did not justify withdrawing protection; two judges dissented and considered the exemption lawful in the circumstances.
issues.conclusion: By majority, the exemption order was ultra vires and void because the stated reasons were not germane to the legislation’s purpose; the appeal was dismissed. Two judges would have allowed the appeal and upheld the order.
issues.legal_principle: The exemption discretion must be exercised consistently with the policy and purpose of preventing unreasonable eviction and controlling rents. An individual order may be reviewed for discrimination, reliance on irrelevant grounds, or mala fides. The mere expiry of a tenancy, a tenant’s refusal of a longer lease, and the tenant’s exercise of statutory protection do not by themselves justify exemption; the tenant’s ability to obtain alternative accommodation for the relevant business is material. The majority applied Article 14 and the guidance principles in Ram Krishna Dalmia v. Justice Tendolkar, [1959] SCR 279, and Sardar Inder Singh v. State of Rajasthan, [1957] SCR 605. The dissent considered all relevant circumstances, including whether eviction would be unreasonable and whether the protection could enable exploitation, and concluded the order was within the statutory purpose.

predicates.individual_building_exemption: The government exempted a particular building from protections otherwise available to its tenant.
predicates.tenant_protected_after_lease_expiry: A tenant remained in possession after a fixed-term lease ended under a statutory protection against eviction.
predicates.exemption_reasons_rely_on_expiry_or_exer: The government relied on the lease ending or the tenant's continued possession under statutory protection as grounds for exemption.
predicates.relevant_alternative_accommodation_not_c: The government did not consider whether the tenant could obtain alternative premises for the business conducted in the building.

issues.definition: When an individual exemption relies on a tenant's protected post-lease possession and the government fails to consider relevant alternative accommodation, the exemption order is invalid.

issues.legal_issue: A court may review an individual exemption order and set it aside when it is discriminatory, based on irrelevant grounds, mala fide, or beyond the authority granted, even if the order is administrative.
material_facts: The government exempted a specified building, thereby removing the tenant’s statutory protection against eviction.
The tenant challenged the order as discriminatory and beyond the purpose of the exemption power.
The majority concluded that the order’s legality could be reviewed and that the court could set aside an ultra vires order affecting a person’s rights.
issues.conclusion: The order was amenable to judicial review, and the court had power to set it aside if it violated equal protection or exceeded the authority granted, even if it was administrative rather than quasi-judicial.
issues.legal_principle: Article 226 permits review of individual exemption orders where they affect fundamental rights or exceed the power conferred, and review is not barred merely because an order is executive or administrative. The stated grounds for review include discrimination, reasons not germane to the legislation’s policy and purpose, and mala fides. The Court relied on Article 14 and the principles in Ram Krishna Dalmia v. Justice Tendolkar, [1959] SCR 279, and Sardar Inder Singh v. State of Rajasthan, [1957] SCR 605.

predicates.individual_exemption_order: The government made an exemption order concerning a particular building rather than an identified class of buildings.
predicates.order_affects_tenant_protection: The order removed a tenant's protection against eviction.
predicates.challenge_alleges_discrimination_irrelev: A party challenged the order as discriminatory, unrelated to the legislation's purpose, or beyond the government's authority.

issues.definition: An individual exemption order affecting tenant protection is subject to judicial review when a party alleges discrimination, irrelevant purpose, or excess of power.
